drills.q: Given coins with unlimited supply, find the minimum number of coins summing to an amount, or -1 if impossible.
drills.a: dp[w]=min(dp[w], dp[w-coin]+1) forward over capacity for each coin; dp[0]=0, others start at infinity; return -1 if dp[amount] is still infinity.

drills.q: Why must the capacity loop go forward here instead of backward like 0/1 knapsack?
drills.a: Forward iteration lets dp[w-coin] already reflect this coin's use earlier in the pass, which is exactly the unlimited-reuse behavior wanted; backward would prevent reuse.

drills.q: Count the number of distinct combinations (order doesn't matter) of coins that sum to an amount.
drills.a: dp[w] += dp[w-coin] with coins as the outer loop and capacity inner; dp[0]=1. Outer-coins prevents counting different orderings of the same multiset separately.

drills.q: Count the number of ordered sequences (order matters) of numbers that sum to a target, unlimited reuse.
drills.a: dp[w] += dp[w-n] with capacity as the outer loop and numbers inner; dp[0]=1. This deliberately counts 1+3 and 3+1 as distinct sequences.

drills.q: Prove greedy fails to minimize coin count for coins {1,3,4} and target 6.
drills.a: Greedy picks 4 first, then must use 1+1, totaling 3 coins (4+1+1); the optimal is 3+3, totaling 2 coins. Greedy is only safe for canonical coin systems.

drills.q: Items now have a cap of k uses each instead of unlimited. How do you adapt the unbounded template?
drills.a: Do not use the plain forward-iteration unbounded template as-is; decompose each item into O(log k) power-of-two meta-items and solve as 0/1 knapsack with backward iteration on the expanded item list.
